title: Add an Android app shell with a MediaCodec decoder
author: tzhazuma
body:
This adds `apps/filmcraft-android`: a Gradle project that hosts the existing egui UI inside an `android-activity` window, plus the platform seams the desktop shell normally supplies — and the MediaCodec hardware decoder behind them.

The engine, the UI and the theme are untouched; `apps/filmcraft` is not compiled, so its `rfd`, `cpal`, `muda` and platform code never enter the graph.

## What the shell does

- **Entry point** — the Rust crate builds as `libmain.so` and is loaded with `System.loadLibrary`; `android_main` is the usual `android-activity` entry.
- **File pickers** — FilmCraft's `HostHooks` (`pick_files`, `pick_open_file`, `pick_open_project`) start the Storage Access Framework instead of `rfd`. A blocking picker cannot answer inside the frame that asks, so the hook answers "nothing picked" and a worker starts `ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT`; the Activity copies the chosen files into `<filesDir>/import/` and the paths come back over the app's own control channel as the *desktop* `file.import` command. Saves answer with a scratch path in `<filesDir>/export/` and are published to the `ACTION_CREATE_DOCUMENT` destination afterwards.
- **Storage** — `AndroidApp::internal_data_path()` is the data directory (autosave, crash log, preferences, imports and exports).
- **Hardware decoding** — `crates/platform` gains an Android arm: an `AMediaCodec` decoder for H.264/HEVC, wrapped in the same `HybridDecoder` as the macOS backend so a mid-stream failure falls back to software. Streams it cannot honour (VP9/AV1, >10 bit, non-4:2:0, interlaced, or a codec the device only has in software) are declined with `note_hw_declined()`, so registering never makes a file undecodable. 10-bit output is converted to the same `PixelData::Yuv16 { bits: 10 }` the VideoToolbox backend produces.
- **Self-test** — a background thread decodes three embedded 320×240 clips (H.264, HEVC, HEVC Main 10) through the engine's own `make_video_decoder()` path and logs the decoder, picture count and hardware…

title: fix(av1): turn a frame worker panic into a decoding error instead of a hang
author: vangel76
body:
## What

A panic while decoding a frame on a frame worker no longer hangs the decoder. The caller gets `Error::Invalid("decoder panicked")` from `decode`/`flush_result`.

## Why

`run_job` had no `catch_unwind`, and nothing set the job's slots during unwind. With frame workers (threads > 1, which is what `Decoder::new()` gives `crates/codecs`), a panic from hostile input killed the worker with its slots unset. `Slot::wait` (in `submit` and `flush_result`) then blocked forever. With one thread the panic propagated to the caller.

## How

- `run_job` runs `decode_frame` under `catch_unwind`. A caught panic goes through the existing error path, which sets `Err` on both the reference slot and the picture slot.
- The worker thread stays alive. Tile and post-filter panics on the rayon pool are covered too, because `pool.install` re-raises them on the frame worker.
- With one thread the caller now gets the same error instead of a panic.
- Valid streams are unaffected.

## Tests

- New unit tests in `decoder.rs` embed a 27-byte libaom key frame, so they need no ffmpeg. A test-only flag makes the frame job panic.
  - With threads 1 and 3, decoding returns the error within a 60 s deadline.
  - The decoder decodes the next key frame normally after the panic.
- Without the fix, the threaded case fails on the deadline and the recovery test hangs.
- `fuzz_hostile`: the comment now matches the behaviour. Panics are caught and become errors, and the panic hook still counts them as failures.
- New fuzz seeds, all small and 3 frames:
  - libaom 4:4:4, 4:2:2 10-bit, 12-bit, monochrome, screen content (`tune-content=screen`), and multi-tile (256x128, 4x2 tiles).
  - SVT superres and film grain.
- Each seed is now checked to decode without error, with 1 and 3 threads, before it is mutated.
- The whole release sweep (10 seeds, 300 random rounds each) takes 90 s. The 600 s deadline is unchanged.

title: perf(av1): CDEF on padded rows per 64x64 filter block
author: vangel76
body:
## What

CDEF (`crates/av1/src/cdef.rs`) changes in four ways:

- **Padded input per filter block.** The padded i16 input is built once per 64x64 filter block and plane. Before, a 12x12 i32 buffer was filled one sample at a time for every 8x8 block, with an availability test on each sample. Now CdefAvailable is settled once per row (above or below the frame) and once per column range (left or right edge), and the available part of each row is a straight copy.
- **Early skip.** A 64x64 filter block is skipped before any sample is touched when its cdef_idx is -1 or all of its 8x8 blocks are skipped. A plane is skipped when its strengths are zero. The luma direction search runs only when a primary strength needs it.
- **No needless frame copy.** The output frame is copied from CurrFrame only when at least one block will be filtered. Before, the copy was made first and then thrown away.
- **Faster direction search.** It adds whole rows into the line sums at the right offset, so it vectorises, instead of scattering each sample into eight partial sums.

The fast all-taps-available i16 filter is unchanged. It now reads straight from the per-block buffer. The edge path keeps the per-tap availability sentinel and still reads the centre sample from CurrFrame.

The full-frame copy itself remains when something is filtered:
- Loop restoration still needs the pre-CDEF frame.
- Inside cdef.rs, the only option would be a fresh frame plus a copy per band. That zeroes and then copies, so a single thread gains nothing.

The cheaper `Plane::clone` is handled separately in `frame.rs`.

## Why

CDEF was 28% of intra and 14% of gop decode time. Most of that went into building the padded buffer sample by sample and into the scalar direction search.

## Numbers

Release build, `perf::decode_throughput`, single thread, thread CPU clock. Base and branch runs alternate. Each figure is the median of 3 runs (2160p: 4 runs). The machine was loaded, so total fps is noisy; the CDEF stage time is t…

title: perf(av1): full-pel copy path for motion compensation
author: vangel76
body:
Part of #3102.

## What

- **Full-pel copy path.** In `predict_inter`, an unscaled single-reference block whose motion vector lands on whole samples in both directions now copies the reference rows straight into the frame. The block must also be non-compound, not inter-intra and not OBMC. Before, both filter passes ran through `tmp` and `pred_buf`, and then the result was clamped and written out. With the identity phase, `Round2(128 * Round2(128 * v, InterRound0), InterRound1) == v` holds for every bit depth:
  - bd ≤ 10: `(128 * (v << 4) + 1024) >> 11 = v`
  - bd 12: `(128 * (v << 2) + 256) >> 9 = v`

  The copy keeps a `min(max)`, so it matches the old clamp even for out-of-range reference samples. Intra block copy and a missing reference still take the old path, because their source is the frame being written.
- **OBMC.** The neighbour jobs live in a fixed `[_; 8]` array (at most 4 above and 4 left, in the same order) instead of a `Vec` allocated per call. The blend works on row slices instead of per-sample `Plane::at`/`set`.

## Not done

- **The i16 `tmp`/`pred` item** from the issue: skipped. The value ranges are not proven and the change was not measured.
- **An identity-phase shortcut inside `mc_unscaled`** (`pred = v << InterPostRound`, which also covers compound and OBMC neighbours): tried and dropped. Against this PR's copy path it showed no consistent direction (7-run medians, single-thread fps):

  | fixture | copy path | + shortcut |
  |---|---|---|
  | gop | 47.2 | 46.6 |
  | 10bit | 37.0 | 40.9 |
  | hq | 16.7 | 16.0 |
  | tiles | 56.3 | 54.2 |
  | 2160p | 14.1 | 14.0 |

## Verification

- **New unit tests in `inter.rs`:**
  - `subpel_phase_zero_is_identity` checks that phase 0 is the identity for all six filter sets, including the reduced 4-tap sets used for w ≤ 4.
  - `fullpel_copy_matches_filter_path` checks the copy against the per-sample 8-tap process of 7.11.3.4 and against `mc_unscaled`. It covers bit depths 8/10/12, every w × h in {2..128}², …

title: effect controls: drag a transition's cut to move it with the transition
author: dotCooCoo
body:
A selected transition's own timeline in Effect Controls (#577) slides the transition and resizes it from either end, but its cut line cannot be dragged. Premiere Pro's help describes this under "Move a cut and transition together" (https://web.archive.org/web/20241230234826/https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere-pro/using/modifying-customizing-transitions.html): dragging the cut line over the transition changes the clips' In and Out points without changing the length of the sequence, and the transition moves with the cut.

- In Effect Controls, a press on the cut line where it crosses the transition (3 px either side, outside the zones of the transition's ends) grabs the cut. While it is dragged, the clips and the transition are drawn where the rolling edit would put them, with the same limits as `timeline.roll` (the clips' media, one frame left in each clip, linked clips when Linked Selection is on). On release, one `timeline.roll` moves the cut, so the drag is one undo step.
- A rolling edit now stops where the transition on its cut would leave one of its two clips. Before this change, rolling a cut close to the start of the first clip moved the transition over the start of that clip (or past the end of the second clip). This also changes the Rolling Edit tool in the Timeline.
- When a ripple trim, a slide or a ripple speed change moves a cut far enough that the transition on it would leave its two clips, the transition is moved back within them and shortened when the clips are now shorter than it. title: perf(av1): loop restoration per stripe with row buffers and box sums
author: vangel76
body:
## What

Loop restoration (`crates/av1/src/restoration.rs`) now works on segments of rows instead of 4x4 blocks. A segment is a run of rows that shares a stripe and a restoration unit row. For each segment:

- **Source rows are built once.** The segment's source rows are copied once into a padded buffer: 3 extra rows above and below, 3 extra columns left and right, with columns clamped at the frame edge.
  - The stripe rule of the get source sample process (7.17.6) is applied per row. Rows outside the stripe come from the pre-CDEF frame, clamped to 2 rows beyond the stripe. Rows inside come from the CDEF frame.
  - The order is the same as before: clamp to the plane first, then pick the source.
  - Buffers are never shared across a stripe boundary.
- **Wiener** runs its horizontal pass once per row and unit (before: 10 rows for every 4 output rows), then the vertical pass.
- **Self-guided** computes A and B once per position, for the rows and columns around each unit, from column box sums slid along the row. Before, each 4x4 block recomputed a (2r+1)² window for 36 positions. Pass 0 computes A and B only on the odd rows it reads. The centre sample is still read straight from the CDEF frame.

The arithmetic per sample is unchanged. The box sums fit in i32. `p * s` and `b2` stay in i64.

## Why

Loop restoration was 8-12% of decode time (12% on the gop fixture). The cost was redundant work: the Wiener horizontal pass repeated rows, every box window was recomputed, and each tap went through a clamping, branching sample function.

## Numbers

Release build, `perf::decode_throughput`, single thread, thread CPU clock. Base and branch runs alternate. Each figure is the median of 3 runs.

| fixture | restoration ms/frame before | restoration ms/frame after | fps before | fps after |

title: perf(av1): drop redundant whole-frame copies in Plane::clone and the output path
author: vangel76
body:
## What

This removes the redundant whole-frame copies listed in #3097, in `frame.rs` and `decoder.rs`.

- **`Plane::clone`** took a zeroed buffer, which memsets the whole plane, and then copied over it, so every sample was written twice. It now takes a recycled or new empty buffer from the same plane pool and uses `extend_from_slice`. The CDEF and loop restoration clones (`cdef.rs`, `restoration.rs`) go through this path, so they get cheaper without touching those files. Whether those clones are needed at all is covered by #3103 and #3104.
- **Second copy of every shown picture.** `Slot::wait` returned a clone of the `Arc` and the slot kept its own, so `Arc::try_unwrap` in `Output::take` never succeeded. Every shown picture was deep-copied again on the caller thread. The picture slot has a single consumer, so it now holds a plain `Picture`, and `Output::take` moves it out with a new `Slot::take` (`Option::take` under the lock).
- **`load_previous_segment_ids`** cloned `segment_ids` and then copied the clone again. It now copies directly.
- **`motion_field_estimation` / `project()`** cloned the whole `FrameHeader` and `SequenceHeader`, plus a `RefInfo` and an `Arc`, on every call (up to 5 per frame) only to satisfy the borrow checker. They now split the borrow of `FrameShared`.

Output is bit-exact.

## Measurements

These come from the crate's `perf::decode_throughput` test: single thread, thread CPU clock, fps.

- The machine is shared with other builds. Separate before/after sessions varied by up to ±30%.
- These numbers are from an interleaved A/B run instead: base and patched test binaries alternated 5 times. Each run is already the best of 3, and the table shows the median of the 5.

title: perf(av1): inverse DCT with compile-time size and a DC-only path
author: vangel76
body:
## What

- `inverse_dct` dispatches on the length to `inverse_dct_n::<N>`, so all the `n >= ...` stage checks are resolved at compile time. The bit reversals (`brev`) come from a const table instead of a bit loop per element and per butterfly, and `cos128` is a single load from a 256-entry table built at compile time from the spec's `COS128_LOOKUP`. Same arithmetic, same step order.
- DC-only fast path: for a DCT_DCT block with `eob == 1` (only the DC coefficient), the row pass has one non-zero row and every column gets the same input. `transform_dc_only` transforms that one row and one column with the same `[i32; L]` lane arithmetic as the full transform, and replicates the column. If the row output is not flat, it falls back to the full transform, so the result is bit-identical by construction.

## How verified

- New unit test `dc_only_matches_full_transform`: every transform size, 8 and 10 bit, several DC values including the clamp limits, fast path == full transform.

title: perf(av1): cheaper dequantisation per transform block
author: vangel76
body:
## What

- `coeffs` no longer clears `Quant[]` (up to 1024 values) for every transform block, including all-zero ones. `reconstruct` takes each value as it reads it (`mem::take`), so the buffer is all zero again before the next block. Only positions inside the tw x th area that `reconstruct` walks are ever written, so this invariant holds.
- The division by dqDenom (1, 2 or 4, applied to a non-negative value) is a shift.
- New oracle fixtures with quantiser matrices (SVT-AV1 `enable-qm=1:qm-min=0:qm-max=8`): `intra_qmatrix_noise` (8 bit) and `inter_qmatrix_10bit`. `trace_headers` shows `using_qmatrix = 1` with qm levels 4, 9, 11 and 12. Both are bit-exact against libdav1d before and after this change, so the README no longer lists qmatrix as untested.

## Not included

The issue also suggests walking only `scan[0..eob]` in dequant and re-zeroing only the written positions of `dequant` and `levels`. I implemented and measured it. It is bit-exact, but it was slower: about +2% cycles on perf_1080p_gop_hq and +1.3% instructions. The scattered scan-order accesses and the extra re-zero loops cost more than the vectorised clears they replace. Re-zeroing only `levels` was also a net loss (+0.4% instructions on gop_hq). Both are left out.

title: audio-dsp: filter channel pairs together in the settled EQ cascade
author: vangel76
body:
## What

`BandBank`'s settled path (no parameter glides) ran the band cascade one channel at a time: channel, then sample, then band. Each band's biquad recurrence is latency-bound, so the inner loop had a single dependency chain. Channels that need filtering are now processed in pairs, so the L and R recurrences of each band run in the same inner loop. A leftover odd channel uses the old single-channel loop, and channels that take the transparent fast path are unchanged.

The per-channel arithmetic is the same operations in the same order, including the `x += m * (y - x)` mix step, so the output is bit-identical. This covers `parametric_eq`, `parametric_eq_full`, `simple_eq`, `graphic_eq_10/20/30` and `notch_filter`.

It compares every sample by `to_bits` against `process_reference`.
- A/B against upstream/main on 60 s of 48 kHz stereo noise plus tone: 0 differing bits for every effect below.
- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test --release -p filmcraft-audio-dsp` (including the ffmpeg loudness oracle).

title: audio-dsp: remix analysis with sparse mel weights and precomputed norms
author: vangel76
body:
`remix::analyze` did quadratic work it did not need to do:

- **Mel bands.** For every STFT frame, each of the 26 mel bands scanned all bins, recomputing each bin's frequency and its triangle weight. Each bin falls in at most two bands. The filterbank is now built once per analysis (`mel_weights`) as a per-band list of `(bin, weight)` in increasing bin order. The weights use the same expressions as before. The terms that are skipped are exactly `+0.0`, so the band energies are unchanged.
- **Similarity matrix.** Both vector norms were recomputed for every pair, and all m² cells were filled although the matrix is symmetric. The norms are now computed once per beat (`fill_similarity`), and each pair fills both of its cells. The dot product sums in the same order, and `na * nb == nb * na` in IEEE arithmetic, so every cell keeps its value.

The output is bit-identical. `sparse_mel_bands_and_symmetric_similarity_are_bit_identical` keeps the old band and similarity code under `#[cfg(test)]` and compares `to_bits` on generated music at 8, 11.025, 22.05, 44.1, 48 and 96 kHz. At 8 and 11.025 kHz the Nyquist frequency is below 8 kHz, so the other `fmax` branch is covered too. The test also covers silent (all-zero) feature vectors. One caveat: with non-finite magnitudes (NaN/inf input), the old code also spread `0 * inf = NaN` into bands that do not cover the bin, and the new code does not.

**Timing.** `remix::analyze` on 60 s of 48 kHz stereo test music (`test_music(48000, 120, 30, 1)`), release build, thread CPU time. Each run is the median of 5; I alternated base and patch over 5 rounds.

| | median of rounds | range |
|---|---|---|
| main (bfc23840) | 295.5 ms | 292.8 to 410.6 ms |
| this PR | 215.2 ms | 210.3 to 218.8 ms |

That is about 27% less CPU time per analysis.

title: audio-dsp: step the resampler's source position instead of dividing per sample
author: vangel76
body:
`StreamResampler::process` (the live playback path when the device rate differs from the sequence rate) computed every output sample's source position with an i128 `div_euclid` and `rem_euclid`.

Now one division per block seeds the position at the block's first output frame. An integer accumulator then steps it by `from / to` and carries the remainder `from % to`. That gives the same source index and remainder for every frame, and the fraction is computed from the remainder with the same `(rem as f64 / to as f64) as f32` as before. The frame index uses wrapping adds, which match the old `as i64` truncation in every case, so debug builds cannot hit a new overflow panic. The three per-block position calls (first, last and next frame) still use the exact i128 form.

The output is bit-identical. `stepped_source_positions_are_bit_identical_to_per_sample_division` keeps the old `process` under `#[cfg(test)]` and compares the output with `to_bits`, and also checks that the source pulls are the same. It covers:
- rates 48k to 44.1k, 44.1k to 48k, 96k to 48k, equal rates, 48k to 96k, 44.1k to 22.05k, 7 to 384k and 176.4k to 1001
- blocks of 1, 7, 333, 512 and 64 frames
- seeks to negative and very large output positions

This PR covers only the per-sample division from #3132:
- Buffer reuse is left out. The per-block `dst` and `pull` allocations and the `drain` memmoves need an API change that touches ui-egui.
- The quality question is left out. Linear interpolation against a sinc/polyphase filter would change the output and is a separate decision.

**Timing.** 60 s of 48 kHz stereo converted to 44.1 kHz in 512-frame output blocks. The pull closure copies source slices, as the mixer's callback would. Release build, thread CPU time. Each run is the median of 5; I alternated base and patch over 7 rounds.

| | median of rounds | range |

title: audio-dsp: wrap LFO phases and delay-line indices without modulo
author: vangel76
body:
## What

This PR covers the output-identical part of #3125.

- `Lfo::phase` wrapped `phase + offset` with `rem_euclid(1.0)`, which calls `fmod` on every LFO read (six per stereo sample in the chorus). A new `wrap_phase` returns `p` for 0 <= p < 1 and `p - 1.0` for 1 <= p < 2. Every other value, such as a chorus with more than four channels or NaN, still goes through `rem_euclid`. For 1 <= p < 2, `p - 1.0` is exact (Sterbenz), and `fmod` is exact too, so the result is the same bits. The flanger's special-mode `(p + 0.5).rem_euclid(1.0)` uses the same helper.
- `DelayLine::read` did two integer `%` per read. With `w < len` and `di <= len - 3`, the first index is in `[2, 2·len − 2]` and needs at most one subtract. The second index is the first minus one, wrapped.

The Chorus LFO change from the issue (updating the LFO less often, or using a rotating phasor instead of six `cos` per sample) is left out on purpose. It changes the output, and I'd rather keep this PR bit-identical, so the issue stays open for it.

- New test `wrap_phase_matches_rem_euclid`: compares `to_bits` against `rem_euclid` for edge values (±0, 1, 2, 3, −1, huge, ±inf, NaN and their neighbouring floats) and 100k random LFO phase plus offset sums in 0..3.

title: audio-dsp: vectorisable true-peak interpolator
author: vangel76
body:
## What

The true-peak interpolator (`oversample.rs`) summed each 16-tap polyphase branch with one sequential f32 `sum()`, which the compiler cannot vectorise. It now sums into eight partial accumulators and adds them pairwise at the end. The interpolator drives the true-peak part of `LoudnessMeter` and the Limiter's true-peak detection.

## Why

Profiling showed the interpolator was 97% of `LoudnessMeter` time and 72% of the Limiter. Export runs the meter up to twice, and the UI meters run it continuously.

## Numbers

Setup: 60 s of 48 kHz stereo in 512-sample blocks, release build, thread CPU time. Base and branch binaries were run alternately, 7 rounds, each round the median of 3 runs. The table shows the median over the rounds. The machine had other load.

| | base | branch | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LoudnessMeter` | 142.2 ms | 104.1 ms | -27% |
| `limiter` (defaults) | 173.9 ms | 122.4 ms | -30% |
| `limiter` (all parameters moved) | 212.8 ms | 177.5 ms | -17% |

These gains are smaller than the 3.1x the issue's prototype suggested. That prototype timed the interpolator alone, while these numbers are for the whole meter and limiter.

## Accuracy

Output changes only at f32 rounding level. A new test keeps the old sequential sum as a reference. It compares the two on white noise, quiet noise and sines up to 23.9 kHz, at factors 2 and 4:

- max abs difference per interpolated peak: 3.6e-7
- max relative difference: 3.8e-6
- max difference of the resulting true peak: 1.7e-6 dB

`tests/loudness_oracle.rs` (against ffmpeg ebur128) prints the same TP values to three decimals on base and branch. The worst |ΔTP| is still 0.053 dB in both. The limiter and dynamics tests pass unchanged.

## Checks

`cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test --release -p filmcraft-audio-dsp` (including the loudness oracle and the premiere tests).

Fixes #3127

title: audio-dsp: defer convolution reverb impulse rebuild to process
author: vangel76
body:
## What

`ConvolutionReverb::set_param` used to rebuild the partition spectra right away whenever `impulse`, `room_size`, `damping_lf` or `damping_hf` changed. The rebuild filters the whole impulse per sample and runs one FFT per partition. Now `set_param` only marks the impulse dirty. The rebuild runs once, at the start of the next `process`. Construction still builds the impulse eagerly.

## Why

render calls `set_if_changed` every block while automation moves. So each changed parameter paid one full rebuild per block, and two automated parameters paid two. With this change, all changes between two blocks cost one rebuild in total.

The rebuild still runs on the audio thread, inside `process`. This is step 1 of #3128. A single automated parameter costs about the same as before, because the rebuild still happens once per block.

## Numbers

Setup: release build, thread CPU time, median of 41 iterations, 5 alternating base/branch runs. Each iteration changes `damping_hf` and `room_size` and then processes one 512-sample block. The block lasts 10.7 ms.

| | base | branch |
|---|---|---|
| two `set_param` calls | 2.79-2.82 ms | 0.6 µs |
| following `process(512)` | 69-71 µs | 1.47-1.53 ms |
| total per block | ~2.87 ms | ~1.50 ms |

## Output

Output is bit-identical. A new test runs two instances through 24 blocks of mixed changes, including two changes of one parameter between the same two blocks and impulse switches. One instance rebuilds after every `set_param`, which is the old behaviour. The other defers. The test compares their outputs with `to_bits`. A second test checks that `set_param` leaves the built impulse key untouched and that the next `process` applies both pending changes.

title: audio-dsp: faster FFT kernel (contiguous twiddles, cheaper first stage)
author: vangel76
body:
The in-crate radix-2 FFT read its twiddles at `k*stride` from a single n/2-entry table and paid bounds checks on every butterfly access. It is the bulk of the cost of pitch_shifter, denoise, dereverb and fft_filter, and a good part of convolution_reverb and sync.

What changed in `crates/audio-dsp/src/fft.rs`:
- Twiddles are stored per stage, contiguously (n−1 entries in total). Each value is computed with exactly the same expression as before (same angle `k*stride`), so the table holds identical values.
- The first stage (twiddle 1 + i·∓0) drops its multiplications by 1, which are exact. The multiplications by ∓0 stay, so signed zeros come out exactly as before.
- The stages work on `split_at_mut` halves and constant-size chunks, which removes the bounds checks.
- The inverse uses a pre-negated twiddle table instead of `sign * w`, which is the same value.

Output is bit-identical. The new test `bit_identical_to_reference_kernel` keeps the previous kernel under `#[cfg(test)]` and compares `to_bits` for every size from 2 to 8192, forward and inverse. Inputs include zero imaginary parts, signed zeros, subnormals and large values.

Timing: thread CPU time, release build. Base (upstream/main) and branch were built into one binary and run alternately, 7 rounds each; the table shows medians. Effects ran on 60 s of 48 kHz stereo noise plus tone in 512-sample blocks.

| | base | this PR | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| FFT 2048 forward | 17.2 µs | 12.5 µs | 1.38x |
| FFT 8192 forward | 90.7 µs | 68.8 µs | 1.32x |
| pitch_shifter (−3.1 st) | 1579 ms | 1351 ms | −14.5 % |
| denoise | 508 ms | 418 ms | −17.9 % |

title: audio-dsp: cheaper gain math in the dynamics effects
author: vangel76
body:
## What

- **Limiter meter:** `Limiter::process` computed `gr_meter = lin_to_db(g)`, a `log10f`, on every sample, but only the value after the block is ever read. It now converts the last gain once per block. A zero-length block leaves the meter unchanged, as before.
- **`db_to_gain` at 0 dB:** returns `1.0` without calling `powf` when `db == 0.0`. 10^(±0) is exactly 1, so the result is identical, and NaN or any other value still goes through `powf`. - **Helper dedupe:** `dynamics.rs` had private copies of `coef` and `lin_to_db` with the same bodies as `util::coef` and `util::lin_db`. It now uses the util versions.

- The `exp(x·ln10/20)` replacement for `powf` from the issue. It changes output by about 1 ulp, and this PR is meant to be bit-identical.
- `essential.rs`'s `coef` and `pow_db`. They work in f64 and nothing else in the crate duplicates them. Folding them into the f32 util helpers would change output.

title: audio-dsp: recover filter state after a NaN or infinite input sample
author: vangel76
body:
## What

`flush` and `flush32` in `lib.rs` zero the recursive state of every IIR element in the crate: `Biquad`, `OnePole`, `AllPass1`, `DcBlock`, the feedback delays and `DelayLine::push`. Until now they zeroed only tiny values, so a NaN or ±inf passed through unchanged. One bad input sample left the filter state non-finite, and the effect produced NaN until `reset()`. They now also zero non-finite values.

For finite values the behaviour is bit-for-bit the same. A test compares both functions with copies of the old ones on ±0, subnormals, the values next to the flush thresholds, ±MAX and 100 000 random magnitudes.

## Why this place

Every IIR state update in the crate already goes through these two functions. Fixing them covers all IIR users with one line each. Sanitising every input buffer at each effect boundary would need a wrapper outside the effects, and it would cost a pass over every block.

## Tests

- `Biquad`, `OnePole` (lp and hp), `AllPass1` and `DcBlock` each get one NaN, +inf or -inf sample among noise. Output must be finite again two samples later. `AllPass1` and `DcBlock` keep the raw input for one sample, so they recover one sample later than `Biquad`.
- `parametric_eq`, `simple_eq`, `graphic_eq_10` and `notch_filter`, with gains set, get one NaN input sample. The next block must be finite.
- Both tests fail on main.

- `binauralizer`

They are not changed here and can be follow-ups.

title: Collapse only XML whitespace in TTML/DFXP cue text
author: Silvertree2010
body:
Found while testing `crates/captions/src/ttml.rs:443 (collect)` (no existing issue): TTML/DFXP import turns non-breaking spaces into ordinary spaces.

## Cause
`collect` in the TTML parser collapsed whitespace with `char::is_whitespace()`, and `clean` trimmed with `str::trim`. Both match Unicode spaces such as U+00A0, U+2009 and U+3000. TTML follows XML whitespace rules, where only space, tab, CR and LF collapse, so no-break spaces in cue text became ordinary spaces on import.

## Fix
Added an `is_xml_space` helper that matches only space, tab, LF and CR. `collect` now uses it to collapse whitespace, and `clean` uses `trim_matches` with it. The regression test checks that NBSP, U+2009 and U+3000 are kept and that XML whitespace still collapses and trims.

## Verified
- Regression test `ttml::tests::only_xml_whitespace_collapses_in_cue_text`: fails on `main` without the fix and passes with it (`cargo test -p filmcraft-captions --lib only_xml_whitespace_collapses_in_cue_text`).

title: audio-dsp: one sin_cos per peak region in the pitch shifter
author: vangel76
body:
The pitch shifter, the slowest effect in the crate, called atan2 and sin_cos for every one of the 1025 bins in every frame (8× overlap).

What changed in `crates/audio-dsp/src/effects/pitch.rs`:
- **One sin_cos per peak region.** Every bin in a region gets the same rotation, so `mag·e^{i(φ+rot)}` becomes `X·e^{i·rot}`: one complex multiply per bin, one sin_cos per region.
- **atan2 only at peaks.** The state keeps the previous frame's complex spectrum instead of a phase per bin. The phase difference is computed only for the peak bins, from `atan2` of the current and the previous bin.

That is two atan2 per peak, not the single `arg(X·conj X_prev)` the issue suggests. With the single form, the result is 0 instead of φ whenever the previous bin is exactly zero (after `reset()` or after digital silence). That change would carry into the accumulated rotation, so it is a behaviour change, not rounding. With two atan2 calls, the peak phases, frequency estimates and rotations stay bit-identical to before. Only the per-bin synthesis changes, at f32 rounding level.

Verification:
- New test `matches_per_bin_reference_to_rounding` keeps the previous per-bin `shift_frame` under `#[cfg(test)]`. It runs both over 40 frames with the ratio gliding up and then down, and checks two things:
  - the rotations are bit-identical;
  - the output spectra agree to within 1e-5 of the frame peak.
- End to end against upstream/main, on 60 s of 48 kHz stereo noise plus tone in 512-sample blocks:
  - at 0 st: max abs deviation 1.2e-7, which is 2.4e-7 of the signal peak;
  - at −3.1 st: max abs deviation 1.8e-7, which is 2.3e-7 of the peak.
  - No sample deviates by more than 1e-5 of the peak. The largest relative deviation on samples above −60 dB of the peak is 6e-5.
- The existing pitch tests and premiere_tests pass unchanged.

title: audio-dsp: two channels per complex FFT in the STFT effects
author: vangel76
body:
Stacked on #3146 (pitch shifter trig). Only the last commit belongs to this PR.

The STFT effects ran a full complex FFT on real data (imaginary part zero), once per channel, forward and inverse. Two real channels can share one complex FFT, as `reverbs.rs` and `sync.rs` already do.

What changed:
- **`effects/stft.rs`**
  - `Spectral::analyse_pair` windows two frames as `a + i·b`, runs one forward FFT and splits the result into both half spectra: `A[k] = (Z[k] + conj Z[n−k]) / 2`, `B[k] = (Z[k] − conj Z[n−k]) / 2i`.
  - `synthesise_add_pair` rebuilds `Y_a + i·Y_b` with Hermitian symmetry and runs one inverse FFT. The real part goes to channel a, the imaginary part to channel b.
  - A `stream` helper drives the streaming sample-major and pairs neighbouring channels that frame on the same samples. It takes a `Pairing` mode:
    - `Full`: shared forward and inverse FFT (dereverb, fft_filter).
    - `SynthesisOnly`: every channel is analysed on its own, exactly like the single-channel path, and only the inverse FFT is shared (pitch_shifter, denoise).
  - Channels that are out of step fall back to the existing single-channel path, which is unchanged and bit-identical. That covers a leftover odd channel, and a channel that fell out of step after a call with fewer channels than configured.
- **The four callers** only supply the per-channel bin processing; the processing itself is unchanged:
  - pitch_shifter (`pitch.rs`);
  - denoise (`restoration.rs`);
  - dereverb (`essential.rs`, `process()` only);
  - fft_filter (`filters.rs`, `process()` only).
- **Glides stay once per frame.** fft_filter still glides its gains on channel 0. pitch_shifter glides its ratio once per frame boundary (the new `first` flag), as before.
- **Invalid samples stay per channel.** A NaN/inf in one channel does not reach the other.

title: audio-dsp: phaser, click remover and binauralizer recover from NaN and inf input
author: vangel76
body:
Stacked on #3144: review after it. Until #3144 merges, this diff also shows its commit. The change here is the last commit.

## What

#3144 made `flush`/`flush32` zero NaN and ±inf, so most effects recover after one bad input sample. Three effects keep state outside `flush`, so one NaN or ±inf input sample still makes them output NaN until `reset()`. This PR fixes all three:

- **`phaser`** (`effects/modulation.rs`): the feedback sample `fbs` was stored raw. With the default feedback of 0, `0 * NaN` is still NaN. It is now zeroed when it is not finite.
- **`click_remover`** (`effects/declick.rs`): a NaN or inf in the analysis span made `r[0]` non-finite. `lpc()` still returned coefficients. Every residual became an outlier, and the NaN interpolation was written back into the look-ahead that the next analysis reads. `lpc()` now treats a non-finite `r[0]` like silent input and returns `false`. That span is left unrepaired, and the bad sample leaves the span after at most three analyses.
- **`binauralizer`** (`effects/special.rs`): the head-shadow filter had its own `if y.abs() < 1e-25 { 0.0 } else { y }`. It now calls `flush32(y)`, so it also zeroes NaN and ±inf.

## Finite input: bit-identical

- `phaser` and `click_remover` only add a branch that finite values never take.
- The old `Shadow` expression is exactly `flush32_reference` from #3144. #3144's `flush_is_unchanged_for_finite_values` test already compares it with `flush32` by `to_bits`.
- A/B check: 60 s of 48 kHz stereo noise plus tone, with 398 added clicks, in 512-sample blocks, at default and at moved parameters. The FNV hash of every output sample's `to_bits` is equal between base and branch for all six runs.

## Tests (in `biquad.rs`, next to #3144's tests)

- `phaser_click_remover_binauralizer_recover_from_non_finite_input`: NaN, +inf and -inf, at default and moved parameters. The output must be finite within two 512-sample blocks after the bad sample's own latency-delayed output.

title: audio-dsp: every effect recovers from one NaN or inf input sample
author: vangel76
body:
Stacked on #3149 and #3148: review after them. Until they merge, this diff also shows their commits and a merge of the two branches. The change here is the last commit.

## What

After #3144 and #3149, every effect recovers from one NaN input sample, except `pitch_shifter`. With one +inf or -inf sample, several dynamics effects never return to finite output. This PR fixes both. It also fixes three similar cases that the wider sweep in this PR found.

Dynamics detectors. The fix zeroes the detector state when it is not finite, at the point where the old code already flushed denormals. Where possible, the old `abs() < eps` test becomes `!(eps..=f32::MAX).contains(&abs)`, so no extra branch is added:

- **`compressor`** (`dynamics.rs`): `level_db` is inf and `curve(inf) - inf` is NaN, so `env` stayed NaN. In RMS mode, `ms` also stayed inf. Both flushes now use the range test.
- **`dynamics_rack`, `multiband_compressor`, `tube_compressor`** (`multiband.rs`): the shared `smooth()` flush and the tube compressor's `ms` and `slow` flushes now use the range test.
- **`guitar_suite`, `vocal_enhancer`** (`special.rs`): their `env` flushes now use the range test.
- **`chorus_flanger`** (`util.rs`): `Envelope::tick` now uses `!(1e-20..=f32::MAX).contains(&env)`. A NaN used to stay in the envelope for good. The output stayed finite, but the transience control was dead after that.

Pitch shifter (`pitch.rs`): `rot` is zeroed when it is not finite. This happens once per peak region per frame, before its `sin_cos`. `rot` is the only state that accumulates across frames. The previous spectrum (`last_re`/`last_im` since #3146) is overwritten completely every frame. A NaN there only makes the next frame's `rot` NaN, and the guard catches that. So the previous spectrum needs no guard of its own. This also covers ratio 1, where `0 * NaN` was NaN.

title: audio-dsp: crossfade convolution reverb impulse changes
author: vangel76
body:
Stacked on #3141: review after it. The diff against main includes #3141's commit; only the last commit (`audio-dsp: crossfade convolution reverb impulse changes`) is new here.

## What

This is step 2 of #3128. Before this change, a change of `impulse`, `room_size`, `damping_lf` or `damping_hf` swapped the new partition spectra in at once, so the output could jump. Now `ConvolutionReverb` keeps the audible partition set when it rebuilds. The next partition block runs the convolution with both sets and crossfades linearly from old to new over its 256 samples (5.3 ms at 48 kHz). From the block after that, only the new set runs.

## How

- The frequency-domain delay line holds input spectra only, so both sets share it. The only extra state is a second partition set (`h_prev`). It is allocated in `new` at full size and swapped with `h` by `mem::swap`, so `process` does not allocate. At 48 kHz this adds 2.8 MB per instance (the Cathedral impulse, 683 partitions × 2 channels).
- The fade is aligned to the partition grid, so the latency stays at 256 samples. The fade completes inside one block.
- Repeated changes before the fade block runs (several small `process` calls, or several rebuilds between two blocks) do not swap again. They rebuild only the new set, so the fade always starts from the set that is audible.
- Changes made before the first block, or after `reset`, still apply at once. Nothing old is audible at that point. This keeps one-shot renders and the premiere tests unchanged.
- The fade is linear, not equal-power. Automation of size or damping gives old and new outputs that are highly correlated, and an equal-power fade would add a +3 dB bump there. For an impulse switch (uncorrelated tails) a linear fade dips by at most 3 dB for a few ms.
- The convolution loop moved into a free function `convolve` unchanged, so it can run for either set.

Rebuilding only changed partitions is not done. Room size resamples the whole impulse, both damping filters are recursive…

title: Timeline: a Rolling Edit drag stops at the roll's limits
author: dotCooCoo
body:
With the Rolling Edit tool, dragging a cut in the Timeline moved the cut with the pointer, past the end of a clip's
media or past the last frame of a clip. On release `timeline.roll` applied the clamped roll, so the cut jumped back
to where the roll stopped. Premiere Pro's help describes the Rolling Edit Tool as moving
the cut between two clips without changing their combined duration
([Trim clips](https://web.archive.org/web/20241225165339/https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere-pro/using/trimming-clips.html)).
#1963 proposes clamping a rolling edit so that it never pulls past the source media or "rubber-bands".

The fix follows the trim drag's `trim_delta` (#653):

- `commands::roll_delta` returns the delta `timeline.roll` would apply, without editing anything. Both use the same
  probe of every linked cut (`clamp_roll_linked`, moved out of the command). When a pair would roll by another amount
  than the chosen delta (a clip whose Out point is past the end of its media rolls the other way), it returns 0 and
  the cut does not move.
- The Timeline's `Drag::Roll` update shows that delta, so the cut stops where the release will put it.

Tests:

- `roll_linked_tests::roll_delta_stops_at_the_start_of_the_media`: a cut rolled far to the left stops 12 frames back,
  where the right clip's media starts, and `timeline.roll` applies the same delta.
- `roll_linked_tests::roll_delta_is_zero_when_a_clip_cannot_roll_by_the_asked_amount`: with the media ending 2 frames
  before the left clip's Out point, +1 and -1 frame rolls report and apply 0, and a -5 frame roll applies -5.
- `timeline_trim_ui::a_cut_rolled_past_its_limit_stops_there`: with the Rolling Edit tool, the demo's City_Night_Drive /
  Desert_Dunes cut dragged past Desert_Dunes' end shows the roll's limit during the drag and lands there on release.
  It fails on `main` (the drag shows the pointer's delta).

Targeted checks:

- `cargo test -p filmcraft-engine --lib roll` (14 passed)
- `cargo test -p filmcraft-ui-egui --test…

title: Faster exports: GPU in the CLI, GPU adjustment layers, --hardware-encoding
author: jozef2003
body:

- **CLI GPU backend:** `filmcraft-gpu` enables no wgpu backend (the desktop app gets them through eframe), so a stand-alone `filmcraft-cli` had no adapter and every export rendered on the CPU even with `gpuRendering: auto`. The CLI now enables the backends itself.

title: h264: implicit 32/32 bi-prediction weights as the rounded average
author: vangel76
body:
## What

`weighted_store` now treats bi-prediction with `w0 == w1 == 1 << logWD` and a zero combined offset as the default rounded average instead of running the i32 multiply/shift path.

## Why

x264's default `weightb=1` makes B slices use implicit weights, and for equidistant references those are 32/32 with logWD = 5. `((32x + 32y + 32) >> 6) + 0` equals `(x + y + 1) >> 1` for every input, so those blocks were paying for the weighted path for nothing. The check is generic (any equal power-of-two weights with offset 0), so explicit tables that happen to carry default weights benefit too.

## Verification

- New unit test compares the shortcut with the full weighted formula for logWD 0, 2, 3, 5 and 7, including offsets that cancel.
- `cargo test --release -p filmcraft-h264` (conformance single-threaded, multi-threaded and draft), `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p filmcraft-h264 --all-targets -D warnings`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`.
- Output md5 unchanged on four extra streams (x264 1080p CABAC and CAVLC long-GOP B, 1080p intra, 2160p high bitrate).

## Numbers

`perf stat -e instructions:u,cycles:u`, `H264_THREADS=1`, base and branch alternating, median of 5 (Ryzen 7800X3D):

| stream | instructions | cycles |
|---|---|---|
| 1080p CABAC long-GOP B | -4.75% | -3.3% |
| 1080p CAVLC long-GOP B | -4.72% | -2.6% |
| 1080p intra | 0.00% | noise |
| 2160p high bitrate (few B) | -0.07% | noise |

Fixes #3160

title: h264: cheaper deblocking boundary-strength derivation
author: vangel76
body:
Speeds up the deblocking boundary-strength derivation for inter macroblocks.

## What

Before, every inter MB looked up the reference picture ids of all four 8x8 blocks (for itself and for each inter neighbour), built 16 `Motion` structs and called `motion_bs` for every segment that has no coefficients.

Now:
- Two blocks in the same slice with equal `ref_idx` in both lists and equal mvs get bS 0 straight away. Within one slice equal reference indices mean the same reference pictures, so this gives the same result as `motion_bs`. Almost all internal edges and most MB edges in long-GOP streams hit this case.
- The picture ids of an MB (`ref_ids8`) are looked up on first use, and only when a segment needs the full comparison (`MbMotion`). Neighbours from another slice always take the full comparison, as before.

The issue also suggests caching the neighbour's ids per row or in `MbState`. With the fast path the lookup is rarely reached, so I left `MbState` and the other files alone.

## Verification

- `cargo test --release -p filmcraft-h264`: conformance fixtures at 1, 3 and all threads, draft mode, and the lane-filter unit test all pass.
- The four perf fixtures decode to their ffmpeg md5s.
- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p filmcraft-h264 --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` are clean.

## Numbers

`perf stat -e instructions:u,cycles:u`, `H264_THREADS=1 H264_BENCH_ITERS=1`, base and branch run alternately, median of 5 (Ryzen 7800X3D). Instruction counts are the main number because the machine was busy.

| fixture | instructions base | instructions branch | change |

| 1080p CAVLC B | 18.823 G | 18.439 G | -2.0% |

title: perf(h264): DC-only inverse transform for blocks without AC coefficients
author: vangel76
body:
## What

`transform::idct4_dc_add` existed but was never called (`#[allow(dead_code)]`). This wires it in:

- `Scratch` gets `blk_ac` / `c_ac`, the subset of `blk_nz` / `c_nz` whose block has a non-zero AC coefficient. `put_luma4`, `put_luma8` and `put_chroma_ac` set it; the DC-only producers (`put_luma_dc`, `put_chroma_dc`) do not.
- `add_luma_block4`, `add_luma_block8` and `add_chroma` take `transform::idct_dc_add::<N>` (the old helper made generic over 4 and 8, with the same bounds handling as the full transforms) when the AC bit is clear, and then only clear coefficient 0 instead of the whole block.

With only coefficient 0 set, every output of the 8.5.12.2 / 8.5.13.2 transform is `d0` before the final `(x + 32) >> 6`, so the shortcut is exact. A new unit test compares it with `idct4_add` / `idct8_add` over 5000 random DC values and pixel blocks.

In `put_luma4` / `put_luma8` the DC coefficient is handled before the loop so the loop's "any AC" flag costs nothing. A first version that did `ac |= k != 0` inside the loop stopped LLVM from unrolling the 64-entry `put_luma8` loop and cost +1.1% instructions on the 2160p stream.

## Numbers

`perf stat -e instructions:u,cycles:u`, `H264_THREADS=1 H264_BENCH_ITERS=1`, `h264dec` example, base (upstream/main bfc23840) and branch alternating, median of 5. Instruction counts are deterministic to within a few thousand between runs.

| fixture | instructions base | branch | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1080p CABAC long-GOP B | 18.22 G | 18.13 G | -0.52% |
| 1080p CAVLC long-GOP B | 18.82 G | 18.67 G | -0.81% |
| 1080p CABAC intra-only | 20.53 G | 20.37 G | -0.76% |
| 2160p CABAC high bitrate | 112.45 G | 112.30 G | -0.14% |

That is below the 1-3% estimated in the issue: the full 4x4 transform is already vectorised and cheap, so the saving per DC-only block is small. Cycles were within noise on a loaded machine.

title: h264: intra prediction from a u8 edge line with per-mode loops
author: vangel76
body:
Faster Intra_4x4 / Intra_8x8 prediction, plus row-wise writes in Intra_16x16 and chroma prediction.

## What

Before, `load_edge` built an i32 `Edge` struct for every 4x4/8x8 block. `pred_nxn` then evaluated the spec formula for each sample, with a runtime block size and a bounds-checked write closure.

Now:
- The neighbours go into one `[u8; 32]` line: the left column reversed, the corner, then the top row. The sample past each end repeats the last one. With this layout every directional mode samples one line: p[x,-1] and p[-1,y] are plain indices, and the special end cases (the last sample of diagonal-down-left, `zmax` in horizontal-up) become ordinary three-tap averages.
- For modes 3-8 the two-tap and three-tap averages along the line are computed once per block. Diagonal-down-left, diagonal-down-right and vertical-left then become one row copy per row. Vertical-right, horizontal-down and horizontal-up pick per sample from the two tables.
- The block size is a const generic (4 or 8). Intra_8x8 reference filtering runs on the same line.
- Intra_16x16 and chroma prediction write whole rows instead of indexing the plane once per sample.

The old per-sample implementation stays under `#[cfg(test)] mod reference`. A new test, `nxn_matches_reference`, compares it with the new code on random samples for all 9 modes and all 16 availability combinations, for both 4x4 and 8x8, including the 128 fill for unavailable neighbours.

## Verification

- `cargo test --release -p filmcraft-h264` passes: the new reference test, the existing intra unit tests, and conformance (including `intra_*`, `constrained_intra` and `no8x8dct`) at 1, 3 and all threads, plus draft mode.
- The four perf fixtures decode to their ffmpeg md5s.
- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p filmcraft-h264 --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` are clean.

## Numbers

title: h264: Decoder::reset keeps the thread pool and cancels in-flight pictures
author: vangel76
body:
## What

`Decoder::reset()` returns the H.264 decoder to its freshly constructed state (parameter sets, avcC configuration, DPB, POC state, pending output) but keeps the rayon pool, the draft setting and the recycled picture buffers. Pictures still being decoded for the old position are cancelled: a flag is checked once per macroblock row, and a cancelled job stops decoding and publishes its remaining rows undeblocked. Every row is still published, so a job waiting on a reference row never blocks. Jobs that have not started yet see the flag and do the same right away. Errors from cancelled jobs go to the old shared state and never reach the new position.

`H264Decoder::reset` in codecs now calls `Decoder::reset()` and re-applies the avcC record, instead of building a new decoder.

## Why

Seeking used to build a new decoder, which spawns a new pool of up to 16 threads, and drop the old one. rayon only stops a dropped pool's workers after their queued work finishes. So up to threads + 2 picture jobs of the old position kept decoding and competed with the new one. This mattered most when scrubbing.

## Files outside decoder.rs / codecs

The row check has to leave the macroblock loops. `PicState` in `slicedec.rs` gets the cancel flag. `mb_done` now returns `Result` and moves the once-per-row work into a non-inlined `rows_done`, which keeps the per-MB path unchanged. The three `mb_done` call sites (two in `slicedec.rs`, one in `cabac_mb.rs`) add a `?`.

## Verification

- Two new tests in `tests/it/robustness.rs`:
  - `reset_mid_stream_matches_a_new_decoder` covers keyint10, open_gop and slices4, with 1, 3 and 8 threads (draft off) plus 8 threads with draft on, and 5 reset points. After each reset it seeks to the next IDR (or back to the start) and checks that the output is identical to a new decoder fed the same access units. It also covers the avcC path.
  - `rapid_resets_do_not_hang` runs 40 rapid resets with 2, 8 and 16 threads on the 120-frame 1080p stream, then de…

title: hevc: table-driven intra availability
author: vangel76
body:
## What

Intra neighbour availability (6.4.1) without the per-sample morton bit loop:

- `zavail` uses a 256-entry z-order table (4x4 units of a 64x64 CTB) and returns early when both locations are in the same CTB. Bits above the CTB size are equal for two locations in one CTB, so one table serves every CTB size.
- `intra_predict` no longer calls `zavail` per 4 samples. The new `zavail_run` returns the availability of the whole left or top reference run as a unit mask: per CTB segment either a single CTB check (other CTB) or a z-order prefix (same CTB, since z-order grows along both directions). The available samples are then copied run by run. Constrained intra prediction still checks the intra flag per unit.

The other `zavail` callers (split/skip contexts, QP prediction, MPM, merge/AMVP neighbours) get the faster lookup too.

## How verified

- Decoder output is bit-exact. While developing, `zavail_run` carried an assert comparing every unit against per-unit `zavail`; it passed across all conformance fixtures (incl. `constrained_intra`, `slices4`, `ctu16`, `ctu32_tu4`, `odd_1918x1078`) and was then removed.
- `cargo test --release -p filmcraft-hevc` (conformance single-threaded, 3 threads, all cores, draft mode), `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p filmcraft-hevc --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`.
- md5 of six libx265 test streams matches ffmpeg with 1, 3 and all threads.

## Numbers

`perf stat -e instructions:u,cycles:u`, `HEVC_THREADS=1`, base and branch alternating, median of 5 (Ryzen 7800X3D). Instruction counts are the primary number; the machine was shared, so cycles are noisy.

| stream | instructions | cycles |
|---|---|---|
| 1080p long-GOP B, WPP | 7.512G -> 7.413G (-1.3%) | -4.5% |
| 1080p long-GOP B, no WPP | 6.906G -> 6.818G (-1.3%) | -4.0% |
| 1080p, 4 slices | 7.199G -> 7.096G (-1.4%) | -3.4% |
| 1080p Main10 | 8.467G -> 8.366G (-1.2%) | -2.6% |

title: h264: const-generic MC kernels, i16 first pass, inline window row copy
author: vangel76
body:
## What

Two commits, both in the motion compensation hot path:

1. **picture.rs (#3157 step 1):** `copy_clamped`, the edge fallback of `copy_line`, is now `#[cold] #[inline(never)]`. Before, LLVM merged the fixed 24/16-byte move and the variable-length fallback into a single libc `memcpy` call with a selected length, so every reference window row went through libc. Now the common path is plain vector moves. In the disassembly `predict_block` went from 18 `memcpy` calls to 0.
2. **inter.rs (#3161):** `mc_luma_win` (width 4/8/16) and `mc_chroma_win` (width 2/4/8) match on the width once and call a const-generic kernel. Loops get fixed trip counts and no bounds checks, and the full-sample copies become fixed-size moves (the old `copy_n` match had also been folded back into a variable-length `memcpy`). The horizontal/vertical 6-tap first pass runs in i16 (range -2550..=10710), which doubles the SIMD lanes. Only the second pass of the centre positions (j, f, q, i, k) stays in i32. The public signatures are unchanged, so callers are untouched.

## Verification

- `fast_luma_matches_reference` (all block sizes, all 16 fractions, on- and off-picture positions) passes. A new `chroma_matches_formula` test checks every chroma width, height and eighth-sample fraction against the bilinear formula.
- `cargo test --release -p filmcraft-h264` (conformance single-threaded, multi-threaded and draft), `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p filmcraft-h264 --all-targets -D warnings`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`.
- Output md5 unchanged on four extra streams (x264 1080p CABAC and CAVLC long-GOP B, 1080p intra, 2160p high bitrate).

## Numbers

`perf stat -e instructions:u,cycles:u`, `H264_THREADS=1`, base and branch alternating, median of 5 (Ryzen 7800X3D). Instruction counts are the reliable number; cycles on this machine move by a few percent between runs.

title: perf(h264): dequantise and place residual coefficients while decoding them
author: vangel76
body:
## What

Before this change, residual levels went into a zeroed `lv` array (64 entries for 8x8). `put_luma4`, `put_luma8` and `put_chroma_ac` then scanned all 16 or 64 entries, mapped them through the zigzag table and scaled them. Now the decoders write straight to the raster position:

- `cavlc::residual_block` and `residual_block_cabac` take a `put(scan_index, level)` closure. It is called once for each significant coefficient only. The closure scales the coefficient and stores it at its raster position in `Scratch::coef` / `coef_c`. So there is no `lv` zeroing, no second full scan and no 64-entry copy for CAVLC 8x8.
- `put_luma4` / `put_luma8` / `put_chroma_ac` are replaced by `luma4_dst` / `luma8_dst` / `chroma_ac_dst`, which return the destination block, level-scale row and dequantiser. The `mark_*` helpers keep the `blk_nz` / `nz_mask` / `c_nz` bookkeeping.
- `transform::Dequant` resolves the qP-dependent shift and rounding once per block. It replaces `scale4` / `scale8`, keeps the `wrapping_mul`, and a new unit test checks it against the 8.5.12.1 / 8.5.13.1 formulas for every qP.
- `residual_block_cabac` is now a const generic over ctxBlockCat (`residual_block_cabac::<CAT>`), so its context offsets, tables and `maxNumCoeff` are constants. It no longer takes `&mut self`.
- Intra16x16 DC and chroma DC still collect their levels in a small array, because they go through the Hadamard transform before scaling.

The index mappings are unchanged: CAVLC 8x8 interleaving (`ZIGZAG8[4 * k + i4]`), the `+ 1` offset for Intra16x16 AC and chroma AC, and `nnz = 1` on all four 4x4s of a CABAC 8x8 block.

The issue also suggested reading the sign and Exp-Golomb suffix bypass bins as one multi-bit read. I left that out. The bins are only adjacent when the level prefix reaches 14 (|level| >= 15). Otherwise the sign is a lone bypass bin between context-coded bins, and `decode_bypass` is already branch-free. It would also need a new function in `cabac.rs`.

## Numbers

`perf stat…

title: hevc: SAO border lines through the vectorised edge run
author: vangel76
body:
## What

SAO edge offset in `crates/hevc/src/filter.rs` now works out once per CTB which of the 8 neighbouring CTBs may be used (inside the picture, and not in another slice or tile when filtering across that boundary is off). Each line is split into the left column, the inner run and the right column. Every part whose neighbours are usable goes through `sao_edge_run`. Before, the first and last line of every CTB and the edge columns went through a per-sample closure that checked the neighbour CTB for each sample.

Samples of transquant-bypass CUs and of PCM CUs with the loop filter disabled now get their deblocked values back after the offset. Band offset therefore always uses `sao_band_run`. The 4x4 block scan for these CUs only runs when the PPS enables transquant bypass or the SPS sets `pcm_loop_filter_disabled_flag`. Otherwise no block can carry the flag.

I did not include the per-row buffer reuse. The only cheap candidate is the two bS buffers in `deblock_row`, and #3177 reworks that function.

## How verified

- Output is bit-exact. The md5 matches ffmpeg on the six perf fixtures (1080p long-GOP with and without WPP, 4 slices, Main10, intra-only, 2160p Main10 high bitrate), single-threaded and with all cores.
- `cargo test --release -p filmcraft-hevc` passes: conformance at 1, 3 and all threads, draft mode, the synthetic tiles/PCM streams, and the `lossless` / `cu_lossless` fixtures, which exercise the restore path.
- None of the streams combines SAO with tiles, because the synthetic tiles/PCM streams have SAO off. So I ran a temporary check that is not part of this PR. For every CTB row of the perf fixtures and all conformance and synthetic streams, it ran the old and the new SAO on the same deblocked samples and asserted identical output. It did this under four perturbations: fake tile layouts with and without filtering across tiles, fake slice boundaries with mixed `slice_loop_filter_across_slices_enabled_flag`, and random no-filter blocks with transquant…

title: hevc: motion compensation without 71-entry slice arrays per call
author: vangel76
body:
## What

Motion compensation no longer sets up a 71-entry `[&[S]; WIN]` array (1136 bytes of pointer/length pairs) for every prediction block, list and component.

- `trows` is gone. The second pass reads `tmp` with stride `WIN`.
- `wrows` is gone. The copied window is read from `win` with stride `WIN`.
- The in-place `rows` array now has exactly `h + T - 1` entries. Prediction block heights are fixed sizes, so `predict_block` dispatches on the window height to a small const-`N` wrapper. Any other height falls back to `WIN`.
- `interpolate` now takes a row accessor (`Fn(usize) -> Option<&[P]>`) instead of `&[&[P]]`. Every caller of a given `interpolate::<P, T>` passes the same accessor type, so there is still exactly one instance per sample type and filter length.

The in-place path still covers windows that cross CTB rows and windows clamped at the top or bottom edge, so streams with small CTBs keep reading in place.

## Not included

The issue also suggests 8-bit uni-prediction rounding straight from the filter pass. That needs a second output path in `interpolate` plus changes at the `slicedec.rs` call site. The estimate was about 1%, and these B streams are mostly bi-predicted, so I left it out of this PR.

title: hevc: even/odd butterfly for the 8..32-point inverse DCT
author: vangel76
body:
## What

The second (row) stage of the inverse DCT for 8x8, 16x16 and 32x32 blocks in `crates/hevc/src/transform.rs` now uses the even/odd partial butterfly. Before, it added a full basis row for every column, for every output row, which is O(N³) on dense blocks.

- The sparse first stage is unchanged. It still adds one basis row per non-zero coefficient. It now also records which columns are non-zero, and the butterfly skips the zero columns. A butterfly level whose odd columns are all zero is a plain copy.
- Intermediates are i16, and the multiplies are i16 x i16. On baseline x86-64 these compile to `pmaddwd`. Before, they used emulated 32-bit multiplies. The `as i16` on the coefficients is safe because scaling already clips them to 16 bits (slicedec.rs, 8.6.2). This decoder has no extended-precision path.
- The butterfly works on columns, so the result is written back transposed.
- `rows_butterfly` is `#[inline(never)]` on purpose. Inlined into the 4-size `inverse` dispatch, LLVM scalarised the loops: intra decode cost +5% instructions in one variant I tried.
- The 4x4 DCT/DST path is untouched.

The transform still reads only the coefficients inside the `max_x` / `max_y` box. Only the first stage reads them, and it is bounded by the box. This makes it compatible with #3188, which clears only that box per transform block.

The sums are exact integers, so the result does not depend on summation order. `matches_the_direct_matrix_product` passes unchanged; it covers sparse and dense blocks, extreme coefficients, every size and both shifts.

## Numbers

`perf stat -e instructions:u,cycles:u`, `HEVC_THREADS=1`, example `hevcdec`, upstream/main vs this branch. The runs alternate, median of 5. libx265 fixtures; all six decode md5-identical to ffmpeg on both builds.

title: hevc: dequantise while decoding residuals, table-driven sig_coeff contexts
author: vangel76
body:
## What

Residual decoding with fewer passes over the coefficient block:

- **Dequantise on write.** Each coefficient is scaled (8.6.3) as it is decoded and stored in a list of (index, value). The separate pass over the bounding box with an i64 multiply and a branch per coefficient is gone.
- **No full-block clear.** The `coeffs[..n*n].fill(0)` per TB (4 KB at 32x32) is replaced by clearing only the coefficient bounding box before the list is scattered into it, since the inverse transform reads only that box. Transform skip and transquant bypass still clear the whole block.
- **DC-only blocks** add the inverse-DC constant straight to the prediction instead of filling the block and running the generic add loop. The intra 4x4 luma DST exclusion is unchanged.
- **Add loops** use a const block size and `max/min` instead of `clamp`.
- **sig_coeff_flag ctxInc** comes from a 16-entry table per sub-block (`SIG_CTX[scanIdx][prevCsbf]` plus the size/position offset), instead of nested matches per coefficient.
- **last_sb / last_pos** come from inverse scan tables instead of linear `position()` searches.
- **Merge candidates** (`mvpred.rs`): the per-PU `Vec` for the temporal/combined/zero candidates is replaced by the existing fixed `[MvField; 5]` list (at most 5 candidates), and the zero candidate is computed directly. Measured alone this is small: about -0.07% instructions on the 1080p long-GOP stream.

Not done: the `coeff_abs_level_remaining` prefix is still decoded one bypass bin at a time. Reading it faster needs access to the CABAC engine state (`value`/`bits`/`range`, private in `cabac.rs`), so it belongs in a separate change.

Note for #3170 (partial-butterfly transform): the box-only clear relies on `inverse_transform` reading only `[0..=max_y][0..=max_x]`, which the current transform does. A new test, `inverse_transform_reads_only_the_coefficient_box`, fails if a later transform starts reading outside that box.

title: hevc: intra planar/angular with const size and hoisted branches
author: vangel76
body:
## What

These changes are all in `crates/hevc/src/intra.rs`. The signature of `predict` is unchanged.

- `predict` now dispatches on the block size to a kernel with a const `N` (4/8/16/32). Planar, DC and angular loops have fixed trip counts.
- Angular prediction works a row at a time. The `fact != 0` check runs once per row, not once per sample. A row with `fact == 0` is a plain copy.
- The `horizontal` check is out of the sample loop. Horizontal modes (< 18) are predicted as vertical rows into a u16 tile, then the tile is transposed into the picture. Before, they wrote one transposed sample at a time.
- The angular reference is no longer a zero-initialised `i32[193]` filled on every call. For non-negative angles the row reads `top`/`left` directly. Negative angles build a small u16 array holding the projected side samples.

author: Silvertree2010
body:
Found while testing `crates/tts-text/src/normalize.rs:455 (time_words, m == 0 branch; called from parse_time at :418)` (no existing issue): TTS normalizer reads on-the-hour times like "9:00 PM" as "nine zero p m".

title: perf(h264enc): keep the winning transform candidate in code_inter
author: vangel76
body:
Part of #3191.

## What

With the adaptive 8x8 transform (Balanced and Quality presets), `code_inter` coded the luma residual as 4x4 into one `Cand` clone and as 8x8 into another, compared the two, and then coded the winner a third time into the real candidate. title: h264enc: SATD on the half-pel plane, const sad8, fixed-size MC
author: vangel76
body:
Kernel overheads in motion search and prediction. The encoded output does not change.

- **SATD on the half-pel plane.** Sub-pel refinement copied every candidate block through `mc_luma` before SATD, including full- and half-sample positions that need no averaging. The new `RefPic::luma_ref` returns a direct view of the plane for those positions and only interpolates into the buffer for quarter-sample positions.
- **const `sad8`.** The 8-wide integer search used the generic runtime-width `sad`. `sad16` and the new `sad8` now share one const-width kernel.
- **Fixed-size MC.** `mc_luma` (16/8) and `mc_chroma` (8/4) dispatch the common widths to an inlined body with a constant width, so the per-row copies and averages compile to fixed-size code instead of memcpy calls.
- **No per-band allocation in `hpel_rows`.** `build_hpel` keeps one scratch buffer per worker (`for_each_init`) instead of allocating two Vecs for every 16-row band.

author: vangel76
body:
## What

- **`threads: 1` now runs on one thread.** The encoder only built its rayon pool for more than one thread. With `threads: 1` the pool was `None`, so the lookahead (`LowRes::new`, `complexity`, `aq_offsets`), the half-pel build and the slice loop fell through to rayon's global pool on all cores. The pool is now built for every thread count. All rayon call sites in the crate already run inside `Pool::install`, so a 1-thread pool keeps all of the work on that one thread.
- **No per-picture `MbInfo` allocation.** The `mbw*mbh` `MbInfo` array is now taken from a small pool and reset, like the frame and half-pel buffers. Arrays come back to the pool when a non-reference picture is finished or a reference leaves the DPB.

title: h264enc: byte-wise CABAC renormalisation
author: vangel76
body:
## What

`CabacEncoder::renorm` shifted out one bit per loop iteration, through `put_bit` and a 32-bit accumulator. It now renormalises in one step with `leading_zeros` and writes whole bytes. A byte of 0xff that a later carry could still change is held back in `outstanding` until a byte that is not 0xff arrives. This is the scheme x264 uses. `bypass` and the end-of-slice flush use the same byte path. The unused `bins` counter is gone.

## Bit-exact

- The output is byte-identical (`cmp`) to main on m1080, t1080 (60 frames, 1080p) and m2160 (30 frames, 4K). I checked each clip at export defaults (Balanced, VBR 20/30 Mbit/s, 2 B-frames, 17 slices at 1080p) and at QP 27, both with `RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1` and multi-threaded: 12 of 12 identical.
- During development, a temporary test fed random decision/bypass/terminate sequences to both the old bit-level encoder and the new one. It used about 8,000 streams, lengths 0-399 plus 1k, 5k and 50k bins, and compared the bytes. All matched.
- Tests in the PR: the decoder round trip now runs at every length from 0 to 299 behind a header byte. The test checks that the header byte is unchanged and the decoder does not read past the end. A new test covers long bypass runs of all 0s and all 1s (long 0xff runs and carries).

## Speed (m1080, export defaults, one thread, pinned core)

The instruction count is unchanged (220.940G vs 220.932G). The gain comes from removing the hard-to-predict branches of the bit loop:

- branch misses: 0.519-0.545G to 0.456-0.483G (about -12%)
- in `perf record`, the CABAC writer (`renorm` + `bypass` + `write_residual`/`write_mb` for the real encoder) falls from 4.7% to 2.8% of cycles
- cycles on the least-disturbed core: 62.6G to 60.8-61.0G (about -2.5%)

title: perf(h264enc): diamond sub-pel refinement and ordered P partition search
author: vangel76
body:
Stacked on #3203: review after it.

Two changes to P/B motion search in `crates/h264enc/src/slice.rs`, one commit each. Both change the bitstream (encoder-side decisions only; the syntax is unchanged).

1. Sub-pel refinement (half-pel and every quarter-pel round) tests a 4-point diamond instead of the 8-point square.
2. P partitions: 8x8 is searched first, and 16x8 / 8x16 are searched only when 8x8 beat 16x16 (x264-style ordering). Previously all three got a full search whenever the 16x16 cost was above the threshold.

title: h264enc: branch-free u32 quantisation
author: vangel76
body:
## What

`quant4` and `quant8` multiplied in i64, used a per-coefficient `if v < 0` branch, and `quant4` used a variable start index for `skip_dc`. This is slow on two counts: 64-bit multiplies do not vectorise on x86-64, and the sign branch mispredicts on noisy residuals.

- `mf4` and `mf8` are now `u32` tables. Every value fits in 16 bits; `mf8` is at most 20972.
- `quant4`: `|v| * mf + f` is computed in u32. 4x4 residual coefficients stay below 2^14, so the product stays below 2^28.
- `quant8`: the 8x8 coefficients here are unnormalised (`A x A^T` with the basis scaled by 8) and reach 2^20, so `|v| * mf` needs about 36 bits. Instead of new rounding tables, `|v|` is split at bit 8: `(256*hi + lo) >> qbits == (hi + (lo >> 8)) >> (qbits - 8)`. Both partial products then fit in u32, and the result is exactly the old one.
- `skip_dc` is handled by quantising all 16 coefficients and then restoring `c[0]`. The loops are straight-line, branch-free code.
- The clamps (`min(0xffff)`, `min(0xff_ffff)`) are far above any reachable coefficient. They only guarantee that the u32 arithmetic cannot overflow on arbitrary input.

## Bit-exact

The issue allowed the 8x8 path to change rounding. The split multiply makes it unnecessary, so the bitstream does not change and no BD-rate sweep is needed.

- `quant4_matches_i64`: compares against the old i64 implementation for every QP, three deadzones, every magnitude below 2^16 at every position, with and without `skip_dc`.
- `quant8_matches_i64`: same comparison for every QP and deadzone, every magnitude below 2^21 (rotated over positions), plus random blocks.
- Encoded output is byte-identical (`cmp`) to main on m1080, t1080 and m2160, at export defaults (VBR) and at QP 27, single-threaded and multi-threaded: 12 of 12 identical.

## Speed (export defaults, Balanced, VBR, 2 B-frames, one thread, median of 5 alternating runs)

| | fps | cycles | instructions | branch misses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| m1080 main | 4.50 | 62.6G | 220.9G | 0…

author: marcoarnulfo
body:
Program: drag a marquee or Shift-click to select several mask vertices, then drag any of them to move them all.

Premiere's masking table ([Masking tool actions and modifiers](https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere/desktop/add-video-effects/work-with-masks/modifiers-and-conditions-for-masking.html)) lists "Multi-select Control Points: Shift, click on each control point", "Marquee-select Multiple Control Points: click + drag a marquee-selection around control points" and "Move Multiple Selected Control Points: click on any selected control point to move all". This PR follows that. With the Selection tool, a drag that starts on the picture outside the mask shape draws a marquee, and the vertices inside it get selected and drawn filled. A drag inside the shape still moves the whole mask. Shift-click adds a vertex to the selection or removes it, and a plain click goes back to one vertex. Adding or deleting a vertex, by any edit or by undo, drops the selection, because the old indices would point at other vertices. Dragging a selected vertex moves the whole selection in one undo step, and Shift still holds the movement to 45°. On the engine side, `masks.moveVertex` now accepts `vertices: [..]`, following `masks.roundCorners`. The move is a single edit, and an out-of-range index leaves every vertex where it was. Graphic layers on the picture keep their own clicks and drags, and a click on empty space still deselects the mask (#683).

The Adobe page doesn't cover two details, so I picked: Shift+marquee adds to the selection, and a marquee that encloses nothing clears it. Happy to switch either. Arrow-key nudging of the selected vertices is left out: it needs keyboard routing that the overlay doesn't have yet.

Closes #3150

Validation:
- `masks_tests::move_vertex_moves_a_list_of_vertices_together`: fails on main (`need \`vertex\``), passes here
- `masks_ui::marquee_and_shift_click_select_vertices_that_move_together`: fails on main (only the grabbed vertex moves), passes here
